blocks.text: If \(AX=\lambda X\), \(X\ne0\), then \(A^mX=\lambda^mX\), so \(\lambda^m\) is an eigenvalue of \(A^m\). More generally \(p(A)X=p(\lambda)X\) for a polynomial p.
\(\det(A^T-\lambda I)=\det((A-\lambda I)^T)=\det(A-\lambda I)\); hence A and its transpose have the same characteristic roots.

For invertible A, \(AX=\lambda X\) implies \(A^{-1}X=X/\lambda\), so the eigenvalue becomes \(1/\lambda\). Since \(\operatorname{adj}A=(\det A)A^{-1}\), the corresponding eigenvalue is \(\det A/\lambda\).
A single nonzero vector cannot be an eigenvector for two distinct eigenvalues: if \(AX=\lambda X=\mu X\), then \((\lambda-\mu)X=0\), forcing \(\lambda=\mu\).
